children: By Fabiana Negrin Ochoa

The global economy has been remarkably resilient in the face of the worst energy shock in decades, but if borrowing costs and inflation go unchecked, a sharp slowdown looms, the International Monetary Fund said.

In its latest World Economic Outlook, the IMF stuck to its baseline forecast for global growth of 3.1% this year. That's down from 3.5% in 2025 but still a relatively solid outcome given the energy market turbulence unleashed by war in the Middle East.

Under that scenario--predicated on assumptions like the gradual normalization of energy flows--the U.S. economy would grow by 2.3% in both 2026 and in 2027, unchanged from last year thanks to private consumption, fiscal policy and technology-related investment. Projections for the eurozone and the U.K. are broadly steady too.
Global headline inflation would reach 4.7% this year, the same as the IMF's July forecast but up from 4.1% last year.
However, if the war drags on for longer, pushing commodity prices even higher and raising borrowing costs further, global growth will be significantly lower and inflation much hotter, the IMF warned.
Borrowing costs have risen sharply in advanced economies, public debt is at historic highs and fiscal cushions thinned by a barrage of crises, said Silvana Tenreyro, chief economist at the IMF.
"The global economy could soon test the limits of resilience," she said.

If a loss of fiscal and monetary credibility in major economies collides with higher commodity prices, the IMF predicts global growth would be reduced by 0.2 and 0.5 percentage point in 2026 and 2027, respectively.
About two-thirds of that hit would come from the lasting disruption to oil and gas markets, as ballooning energy bills sap households' purchasing power and business investment.
More expensive energy would also account for most of the uptick in inflation, which is projected to be 1.1 percentage points higher in 2027.
"To prevent such a scenario, public debt levels need to be put back on a durably sustainable path," Tenreyro said.

Policymakers must contain the immediate risks posed by inflation, debt and financial fragility, the IMF said, stressing the need to reduce borrowing so as to be in a position to support the economy in the event of future shocks.
"Given elevated debt, rising sovereign yields, and pressing spending needs, a renewed focus on rebuilding fiscal space is increasingly urgent," it added.
Monetary policy, meanwhile, should remain firmly focused on stabilizing prices.

Interest rates need to be sufficiently restrictive to return inflation to target in a timely manner, and if commodity price increases and technology-related investment fan cost pressures, central banks need to tighten further, Tenreyro said.

Markets are already bracing for further rate hikes in the coming months, as oil returns to the $100-a-barrel mark, bond yields cling to multidecade highs and expectations of a swift end to the Iran crisis fade.

The AI investment boom has buffered parts of the global economy against higher energy prices but bypassed many other countries that are more exposed to the full cost of the war between the U.S. and Iran.
According to the IMF, 32 economies now account for 95% of global growth, compared with 54 in the April edition of the WEO. Forecast cuts are more widespread, with about 47% of economies downgraded.

"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the fund said.
Not only is resilience distributed unevenly along those two lines, global growth is now heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions, Tenreyro added.
And those reaping the biggest rewards from AI might have the most to worry about on the inflationary front as the investing boom fuels demand.
So far, AI spillovers to core inflation in major economies appear limited, but the threat is worth monitoring as energy prices rebound, rippling out to other commodities.

Global headline inflation rose in August following a short-lived ceasefire, while prices of core goods in some advanced economies have started to reflect the rapidly rising cost of memory chips, the IMF said.
In its baseline forecast, the IMF still expects a cooldown next year, but it edged up its inflation view by 0.2 percentage point to 4.1%.
Still, the potential upside can't be ruled out, the IMF said.

"The constellation of accommodative financial conditions, robust private-sector adjustment, and AI-related investment could carry activity through the war shock and begin to lift productivity," it said.

title: IMF Warns of Global Economic Setbacks as Shocks Test Resilience
